chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from al-'Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from one of them (peace be upon them both) who said:
I asked him about a man who performed Dhihar with his wife five times or more. He said, 'Imam Ali (peace be upon him) said: For each time, there is an expiation.'
He said, 'And I asked him about a man who performed Dhihar with his wife, then divorced her before consummating the marriage with her. Is there an expiation?' He said, 'No.'
And he said, 'And I asked him about Dhihar upon a free woman and a slave girl.' He said, 'Yes.'
It was said, 'If he performed Dhihar in the month of Sha'ban and did not find what to free [a slave]?' He said, 'He waits until he fasts the month of Ramadan, then he fasts two consecutive months.'
If he performed Dhihar while he was traveling, he waits until he returns. And if he fasted and then acquired wealth, he should complete what he began.'
And this narration does not contradict what was narrated...
ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for Dhihar if one cannot free a slave and is traveling?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the specific mechanics of *Dhihar* expiation, emphasizing that each utterance incurs a distinct penalty, a point of nuance in Shia fiqh. It further clarifies the suspension of duties during travel and the continuity of fasting obligations even if wealth is acquired mid-process, ensuring the expiation sequence remains unbroken. The text also confirms the universality of the ruling for both free and enslaved women, highlighting the comprehensive nature of the juristic derivation.
